checkpoint.prompt: The session says your body did its job where you were. What is the work now?
choices: Forgetting that time completely
Teaching your body that home is not there
Staying on guard, since habits keep you safe

checkpoint.prompt: A loud noise at home spikes you to full alert. What does this session call that?
choices: A character flaw
A trained response firing where it is no longer needed
Proof you are not ready

checkpoint.prompt: What is the daily practice this session gives you?
choices: Avoiding stressful rooms
A slow exhale practice that tells your body the threat level here
Pushing through and ignoring the surge

checkpoint.prompt: Same noise, new meaning. What does this session ask you to train?
choices: Never react to noise
The difference between there and home
Avoiding every loud room

checkpoint.prompt: Why rehearse the difference before you are home?
choices: So the body learns a new meaning before the live test
So you can argue you are fine
It is optional filler

checkpoint.prompt: Which practice fits this session?
choices: Name two home sounds that used to mean threat, and rehearse a calm label for each
Stay silent until reunion day
Only practice after a blowup

checkpoint.prompt: How does this session tell you to treat the emotional wave of the first weeks?
choices: Plan around it; do not grade yourself by it
Fight it until it passes
Take it as the truth about how the return is going

checkpoint.prompt: A hard day in week two means what?
choices: The return is failing
You are on the wave the session told you to expect
You need to try harder tomorrow to prove it

checkpoint.prompt: What belongs in a wave-day plan?
choices: A packed calendar to make up for lost time
Sleep anchors, fewer commitments, and a written rule for hard days
Waiting to plan until you feel settled

checkpoint.prompt: Which plan fits the first weeks, per this session?
choices: Pack the calendar to make up for lost time
Few commitments, kept without fail
Wait to commit to anything until you feel settled

checkpoint.prompt: Why few promises instead of many?
choices: Children prefer silence
A kept small promise builds trust; a broken big one costs more
Courts require fewer promises

checkpoint.prompt: You can only keep two standing times this week. The move is?
choices: Promise five and hope
Promise two and keep both
Promise none so you cannot fail

checkpoint.prompt: Who does this session tell you to get to know?
choices: The child you remember
The child in front of you now
The child you hoped they would become

checkpoint.prompt: Your child's interests changed completely while you were away. The session's move is what?
choices: Steer them back to what you shared before
Learn the new world with questions, from the start
Give it time and let them come to you

checkpoint.prompt: Why do questions matter so much at this stage?
choices: They show the child you are studying who they actually are now
They fill awkward silence
They test what the child remembers about you

checkpoint.prompt: What is the rule of this session?
choices: Ask once. Listen longer than you talk.
Ask many rapid questions.
Assume you still know them.

checkpoint.prompt: Which move fits after you ask a real question?
choices: Jump in with advice
Listen longer than you talk, then reflect one thing you heard
Change the subject to your own story

checkpoint.prompt: Why ask before you assume?
choices: Assumptions belong to the child you left, not the one in front of you
Questions impress the court
Listening is optional

checkpoint.prompt: What beats what, in this session's rule for rebuilding trust?
choices: Big and rare beats small and often
Small and often beats big and rare
Words beat actions early on

checkpoint.prompt: Which is a deposit, as this session means it?
choices: A ten-minute call that happens exactly when you said
A large gift on a birthday
A promise about next year

checkpoint.prompt: Why do small deposits work on a child's trust?
choices: Children prefer small things
Each kept promise is evidence, and evidence stacks
They cost less

checkpoint.prompt: What is the session's rule for showing up?
choices: Show up short and steady
Show up rare and dramatic
Show up only when you feel ready

checkpoint.prompt: Which pattern builds more trust?
choices: One long visit after months of silence
Short, predictable contact kept on schedule
Big speeches about the future

checkpoint.prompt: Why does frequency beat intensity here?
choices: Children get bored of long visits
Predictable short contact is evidence the child can count on
Intensity is never useful

checkpoint.prompt: How does this session treat rupture between you and your child?
choices: As normal, with repair as the skill
As rare if you are careful
As proof the return came too soon

checkpoint.prompt: You snapped at your child last night. The session's next step is what?
choices: Give them space for a few days
Own it out loud, briefly and without excuses, and say what you will do differently
Do something fun together and move on

checkpoint.prompt: What does a child learn from watching you repair?
choices: That you are unreliable
That being wrong can be handled honestly
That they can get away with things too

checkpoint.prompt: What is the move when pride wants to wait?
choices: Go first. Keep it short.
Wait until they apologize.
Write a long defense.

checkpoint.prompt: Which repair fits this session?
choices: I was wrong to raise my voice. You did not deserve that.
I am sorry you took it that way.
We both messed up, so we are even.

checkpoint.prompt: Why go first?
choices: It proves you are weak
Repair protects the bond; pride delays the skill
The child should carry the silence

checkpoint.prompt: What does this session have you build before the day comes?
choices: A speech about the future
A first-hour plan, rehearsed
A list of questions for the child

checkpoint.prompt: If the child pulls away on reunion day, the session says that is what?
choices: The answer
The start, not the answer
A sign to give the plan up

checkpoint.prompt: Which first hour fits this session's counsel?
choices: Low pressure, an ordinary shared activity, exits allowed
A big celebration with everyone there
A serious talk about everything that happened

checkpoint.prompt: What is the return, in this course's final frame?
choices: A day you get right or wrong
A season you work, deposit by deposit
A test the child administers

checkpoint.prompt: What carries the return through month three and beyond?
choices: The emotion of the reunion
The routines: standing times, kept promises, fast repairs
The child's forgiveness

checkpoint.prompt: When the old pattern gets tested and you hold, what does the session call that?
choices: Luck
The line holding, which is what change looks like from inside
A sign the work is finished

final_qa.prompt: Describe your body's alarm firing at home or in rehearsal since you started this course: the trigger, what the old response would have been, and what you did instead.
List the small deposits you have running right now: what you promised, to which child and/or significant other, and your record of keeping each one. What is the next deposit you will add?
Write your first-hour plan for the reunion, or describe how the first hour actually went: the setting, your opening move with kids and/or your significant other, and your plan if a child pulls away.
Name the few promises you are keeping this season, and the accountability partner or facilitator check-in that holds you to them.
